title: Climate and Energy
description: Ten calm, factual texts about climate and energy: a wind farm on the plains, a family that sealed their old house, an interview with a forest scientist, heat pumps explained, a town planting shade trees, nuclear power weighed fairly, a solar car race, monks with floating solar panels, a cable theft and a quiet electric bus.

lessons.title: Wind on the Hansen Ranch
lessons.summary: A cattle rancher explains why he agreed to put twelve wind turbines on his land, and what they have and have not changed.
lessons.text:
Dale Hansen has raised cattle on the same land for 40 years. His ranch lies in the southeast corner of the county, where the plains are so flat and open that you can watch a storm coming an hour before it arrives. It is a view Dale has loved all his life, and he never expected to share it with 12 wind turbines.

The company first contacted him 9 years ago. At the time, his sentiment was simple: he did not want strangers on his land. It took two long visits and a great deal of coffee to persuade him even to listen. What finally persuaded him was not a speech about the climate but a sheet of numbers. Each turbine would pay him a fixed amount annually, and 12 turbines would pay more than his cattle earned in a bad year.

"I wanted a realistic picture," Dale says. "Not a dream and not a nightmare." So he asked realistic questions. Would the towers scare the cattle? Would the new roads damage the grass? What would happen if the company went out of business?

The answers were mostly good. The turbines take up only a small part of the land, and the cattle feed right up to the base of the towers. On hot afternoons, they even rest in the long shadows of the blades. The company also promised, in writing, to remove the towers if it ever stopped using them.

Dale has always been interested in mechanics, the science of how machines move, and he soon became friends with the two technicians who look after the turbines. Both studied mechanics at a technical college, and they gladly explain the mechanics of a turbine to anyone who asks. They once took him up the narrow ladder inside a tower, to the heavy steel shaft that turns the generator. The shaft is forged from a single piece of steel, because a part forged in one piece is stronger than one made of several. When there is a breakdown, which happens a few times a year, the technicians climb up and repair it. A breakdown may stop one turbine for a day or a week, but the others keep turning.

Dale calls himself a patriot, and he means it in a practical way: he likes knowing that the power made on his land is used in his own state. Not every neighbor shares that sentiment. One family down the road says the towers spoil the view, and Dale respects their opinion. Being realistic, he says, means admitting the costs as well as the benefits. On nights with strong wind, the blades make a low sound, and a few birds die each year.

Once annually, Dale walks the whole line of towers with the technicians. "Some people see machines," he says. "I see a second crop, one that grows in the wind."

Questions:
Where does Dale's ranch lie?
It lies in the southeast corner of the county.
What finally persuaded Dale to agree to the turbines?
A sheet of numbers persuaded him: each turbine would pay him a fixed amount annually.
What realistic questions did Dale ask?
He asked whether the towers would scare the cattle, whether the roads would damage the grass and what would happen if the company went out of business.
Why is the shaft forged from a single piece of steel?
A part forged in one piece is stronger than one made of several.
In what way is Dale a patriot?
He likes knowing that the power made on his land is used in his own state.

lessons.title: The Winter We Stopped Heating the Street
lessons.summary: A homeowner describes how her family found and sealed the leaks in their old house, and what changed afterward.
lessons.text:
I have to confess something: for 11 winters, I heated the street. Not on purpose, of course. Our house was built in 1926, and by the time we bought it, it had been neglected for years. We neglected it a little more, I confess, because there was always something more pressing to pay for than invisible air.

The air was not invisible to our energy bills, however. Every January, the heating bill was a headache, and every February, it was a bigger headache. The house was never truly warm. My husband wore a hat inside the house, and our daughter developed a winter cough that never quite went away.

Last fall, a friend told us that the city would send someone to check our house for free. The woman who came carried a special camera that shows heat as color. Warm surfaces looked yellow and red on its screen, while cold ones looked blue and purple. She walked slowly from room to room, and the camera told a story we had been ignoring for years.

The worst room was the dining room. Cold air was coming in through the gaps around the wooden trim of the old windows, and under the trim along the floor. In the attic, where there should have been a thick layer of insulation, there was almost nothing. Much of the warm air we paid for was rising straight through the ceiling and out into the sky.

Over the next month, we fixed what she had found. A local company blew insulation into the attic. My husband removed the old window trim, sealed the gaps behind it and put the trim back. We added strips of rubber around the doors. None of it was exciting, and none of it was very expensive.

The difference was clear by December. The dining room, which we used to avoid in winter, became the warmest place in the house, and I now work at the dining table most days. When I worked there before, my hands were cold, I kept getting up to make tea, and my productivity suffered. Now my productivity is better than it has been in years, or at least I have one less excuse.

Our daughter's cough has not returned. Her doctor said that warmer, less damp rooms often help with a winter cough, though she was careful not to promise too much. The bills dropped by about a third. Of course, it was a mild winter, and a mild winter makes everything look better, so the real test will come next year.

There was one last adjustment. We now turn the heat down a few degrees at night. It is a small adjustment, but small adjustments, I have learned, add up.

Questions:
Why had the house become so cold?
It had been neglected for years, both by the old owners and by the writer's family.
What did the special camera show?
It showed heat as color, so cold surfaces looked blue and purple.
What was wrong with the dining room?
Cold air was coming in through the gaps around the old wooden trim of the windows and the floor.
How did the changes affect the writer's productivity?
Her productivity improved, because she no longer had cold hands while she worked at the dining table.
Why will the real test come next year?
It was a mild winter, and a mild winter makes everything look better.

lessons.title: A Conversation with a Forest Scientist
lessons.summary: An interview with a climate scientist who measures how much carbon forests take in, and why she is worried but hopeful.
lessons.text:
Dr. Helen Okoro studies how forests take carbon dioxide out of the air. She spent 6 years measuring trees in the jungle of central Africa, and she now works as a science advisor to the state government. This year, she is also a nominee for a national science prize. We spoke in her office, which is full of maps, seeds and photos of very tall trees.

You spent years in the jungle. What did you actually do there?

Mostly, we measured trees. We measured the same trees again and again, year after year, to see how fast they were growing. A growing tree stores carbon in its wood, so if you know how much wood the jungle adds every year, you know roughly how much carbon it takes from the air.

And what did you find?

That the jungle is still taking in a great deal of carbon, but a little less than it used to, especially in dry years. Moreover, the trees that die in droughts release some of their carbon back into the air.

That sounds alarming. Should we be alarmed?

Concerned, yes. Alarmed, no. In the realm of science, we try to separate what we know from what we fear. What we know is that the planet has warmed by more than 1 degree in the last 150 years, mainly because we burn coal, oil and gas. What we fear, we test.

Could you elaborate on how you test it?

We build computer models. A model is a set of rules, and each rule has a parameter, a number that we have to choose carefully. Let me elaborate with an example. One parameter says how fast a tree grows when the air gets warmer. If that parameter is wrong, the whole model is wrong, so we check every parameter against real measurements from the jungle.

Forgive me for interrupting, but are the models reliable?

Please, interrupt as often as you like. They are reliable enough to be useful, and honest about where they are not. Strictly speaking, no model is perfect. But strictly speaking, no weather forecast is perfect either, and we still carry an umbrella.

What does your work as an advisor involve?

As an advisor, I explain the science, not the politics. If a minister asks me what will happen if a forest is cut down, I answer that question. What the government decides to do is its job, not mine. I am careful not to step outside my realm.

How does it feel to be a nominee for the prize?

Strange, honestly. The prize belongs to the whole team, and moreover, to the trees, which did all the work.

Are you hopeful?

I am. We understand the problem far better than we did 30 years ago, and we know what helps: cleaner energy, and forests that are left standing.

Questions:
What does Dr. Okoro do as a science advisor?
She explains the science to the state government, not the politics.
Why did she measure the same trees in the jungle year after year?
She wanted to see how fast they were growing, because a growing tree stores carbon in its wood.
What is a parameter in a computer model?
It is a number in one of the model's rules that the scientists have to choose carefully.
Did she mind being interrupted?
No. She invited the interviewer to interrupt as often as necessary.
Why does she say the prize does not belong only to her?
She says it belongs to the whole team and, moreover, to the trees.

lessons.title: How a Heat Pump Works
lessons.summary: A shop owner explains, step by step, how a heat pump moves heat into a house in winter and out of it in summer.
lessons.text:
Ana Ruiz runs a small heating shop in our town, and she has had the same conversation hundreds of times. A customer comes in, points at the white box on the wall and asks, "So how does this thing make heat?" Ana always gives the same answer: "It doesn't make heat. It moves it."

People often characterize heat pumps as a brand new invention, but the idea is more than 100 years old. Every refrigerator in your kitchen is a heat pump. It takes heat out of the food inside and releases it into the room, which is why the back of a refrigerator feels warm. A heat pump for a house does the same thing in the opposite direction. In winter, it takes heat from the outdoor air and releases it inside.

That sounds impossible on a freezing day, but even cold air contains some heat. A special liquid in the pipes boils at a very low temperature. Outside, it absorbs heat from the air and turns into gas. A pump squeezes the gas, which makes it much hotter, and the hot gas then gives its heat to the house before the cycle begins again.

What makes the system attractive is its efficiency. In mild weather, a good heat pump can deliver about 3 units of heat for each unit of electricity it uses. As the intensity of the cold increases, it has to work harder, and that number falls. Modern models work well below freezing, but geography still matters. Where winters are very long and very cold, some families keep a second heater for the coldest weeks. In a mild geography, one heat pump is usually enough.

In summer, the system simply runs backward and cools the house, and it does all of this quietly. Ana likes to give a demo in the shop: she turns one on, and customers are surprised that it runs so quietly they can barely hear it. Some of them ask her to repeat the demo, because they are not sure it is running at all.

Ana is a retailer, so she makes her living by selling machines, yet she does not push them on everyone. Many retailers offer a bundle that includes the heat pump, the installation and a few years of service. A bundle is often cheaper than paying for each part separately. Before she will arrange an installation, however, Ana sends someone to look at the house. If the house leaks heat, she will arrange for the leaks to be sealed first. In her view, a heat pump is not a remedy for every problem. If the walls and windows leak, the first remedy is to seal them. Asked to characterize her job in one sentence, she smiles: "I help people keep the heat they already paid for."

Questions:
How does Ana answer the question about how a heat pump makes heat?
She says that it does not make heat; it moves it.
Why does the back of a refrigerator feel warm?
The refrigerator takes heat out of the food and releases it into the room.
How does the intensity of the cold affect a heat pump?
As the cold gets more intense, the heat pump has to work harder and becomes less efficient.
What surprises customers during Ana's demo?
They are surprised that the heat pump runs so quietly.
What does a retailer's bundle often include?
It includes the heat pump, the installation and a few years of service.

lessons.title: Shade for Main Street
lessons.summary: A small town decides to plant a thousand trees, and neighbors, a pastor and a cafe owner help it happen.
lessons.text:
Summers in Millbrook have been getting hotter, and nowhere is the heat worse than on Main Street. It is a wide street of shops with almost no trees, and by 2 o'clock in July, the sidewalks are too hot to touch. The sunshine that people love in April becomes something to escape in August.

Two years ago, the town council made a simple declaration: Millbrook would plant 1,000 trees in 5 years, starting with Main Street. Some people smiled at the declaration, because the town had made promises before. This time, however, the council had a plan and a budget.

The first question was which trees to plant. A local expert explained that the best choice was indigenous trees, the kinds that grew in the area long before the town existed. Indigenous trees are used to the local soil and weather, so they need less water once they are established, and they feed the local insects and birds. The council chose oaks, maples and a few smaller indigenous trees for narrow spaces.

Help came from many directions. The pastor of the church on Main Street offered the church lawn as a place to store the young trees before planting. On planting days, the pastor also opened the church kitchen, and volunteers came in to wash their hands and rest. The owner of the cafe across the street, Grace Lin, brought trays of ham sandwiches and cold lemonade. By the end of the first season, she said, she had made more ham sandwiches than in her whole life.

Not everyone was convinced at first. One shop owner worried that the trees would hide his sign. But trees do more than look pleasant. Their shade can make a street several degrees cooler, and a cooler street brings more customers. By the second summer, people were sitting outside the cafe again in the afternoon, under young maples instead of umbrellas, with the sunshine falling softly through the leaves.

The trees are still small, and they will need 20 years to become what the town imagines. But there are already signs. Last June, a bride and her family stopped on Main Street so that a photographer could take pictures under the oldest oak, one of the few trees that had been there all along. The bride said she had chosen the street because of its new green look. And on any hot afternoon, you can see a dog or two lying on its belly in the shade, its belly pressed against the cool grass.

In the fall, the council held a dinner to show its appreciation for the volunteers. The pastor gave a short speech, Grace provided the food, and the mayor read a letter of appreciation that ended simply: "Thank you for the shade."

Questions:
What declaration did the town council make?
It declared that Millbrook would plant 1,000 trees in 5 years, starting with Main Street.
Why did the town choose indigenous trees?
Indigenous trees are used to the local soil and weather, and they feed the local insects and birds.
How did the pastor help?
The pastor offered the church lawn for the young trees and opened the church kitchen on planting days.
What did the cafe owner bring to the volunteers?
She brought ham sandwiches and cold lemonade.
Why did the council hold a dinner in the fall?
It held the dinner to show its appreciation for the volunteers.

lessons.title: Nuclear Power: A Calm Look at Both Sides
lessons.summary: A newspaper editorial weighs the arguments for and against nuclear power without taking a final side.
lessons.text:
Few subjects divide our readers as sharply as nuclear power. Some see it as the cleanest way to keep the lights on; others see it as a danger we should leave behind. This editorial will not tell you which side to take. Our motive is simpler: to set out the strongest arguments on both sides, so that you can weigh them yourself.

Begin with the case for. A nuclear plant produces almost no carbon dioxide while it runs. Not only does it produce power day and night, but it does so whatever the weather, which wind and solar cannot do on their own. It also needs very little land. Supporters point out that climate change threatens farms, coasts and cities, and that any source of steady, clean power deserves a serious hearing.

Supporters also ask us to count the toll of the alternatives. Burning coal releases smoke that damages the lungs, and over many decades, the health toll of coal has been far greater than that of nuclear power. Measured by the energy they produce, nuclear plants have one of the best safety records of any source.

Now the case against. The first problem is cost. New plants are very expensive, and they often take much longer to build than planned. When a project runs over budget, it is frequently the taxpayer who pays the difference. A taxpayer who pays more for a plant that opens years late has a fair reason to complain. The duration of construction matters for the climate too: a plant that takes 15 years to build cannot cut emissions for the next 15 years.

The second problem is waste. Used fuel stays dangerous for thousands of years. One solution, already being built in northern Europe, is a deep vault cut into solid rock, where the waste can be sealed away. A vault of that kind may be safe, but no human institution has ever planned for such a duration.

The third problem is fear, and it should not be dismissed. Serious accidents are rare, but when they happen, whole towns may have to leave their homes. The trauma of such a move can last for generations, and the distress of not knowing whether one's home is safe is real, whatever the measurements say. Trauma and distress are costs too, even if they are hard to put in numbers.

What we would ask of our readers is a careful separation of facts from feelings, while still respecting both. That separation is difficult, but it is the only fair way to decide. Nuclear power is neither a miracle nor a monster. It is a tool with real benefits and real costs, and nothing in this editorial is meant to threaten anyone's beliefs, only to inform them.

Questions:
What is the motive of this editorial?
Its motive is to set out the strongest arguments on both sides so that readers can weigh them.
What advantage does nuclear power have over wind and solar?
It produces power day and night, whatever the weather.
Why might a taxpayer complain about a new plant?
New plants often run over budget, and it is frequently the taxpayer who pays the difference.
What is the purpose of the deep vault in northern Europe?
It is a place cut into solid rock where used fuel can be sealed away.
What other costs, besides money, does the editorial mention?
It mentions the trauma and distress of people who have to leave their homes after an accident.

lessons.title: The Sunshine Derby
lessons.summary: A twelve-year-old girl builds a small solar car for her school's derby and learns that patience matters as much as speed.
lessons.text:
Every May, the middle school in our town holds the Sunshine Derby. It is a race for small cars, about the size of a shoe box, that run only on power from the sun. The derby is also a showcase for the science class: parents walk between tables where the students showcase their designs, their drawings and their mistakes.

This year, 12-year-old Maya Brooks entered the derby for the first time. Her science instructor, Mr. Patel, gave each student a small solar panel, a motor and four wheels. Everything else was up to them. For six weeks, the car became Maya's main homework. She did her regular homework at the kitchen table, and then she did her derby homework on the floor of the garage.

Mr. Patel has taught for 20 years, and he says the most useful trait in a young engineer is not intelligence but patience. Maya, by her own account, did not have that trait at first. Her first car was so heavy that it barely moved. Her second car was light but fell apart. Each time, Mr. Patel asked her the same calm question: "What did you learn?" Slowly, she began to ask herself that question before he did.

The problem, she discovered, was weight. A tiny panel can produce only a little power, so a light car accelerates faster than a heavy one. She replaced the wooden body with thin plastic from an old food box and moved the panel so that it faced the sun directly. On the last test, the car accelerated smoothly across the garage floor, and Maya allowed herself a small smile.

On race day, the school yard was crowded. When Maya placed her car at the starting line, a cloud moved across the sun, and the car did not move at all. She bit her lip and tried not to stare at the sky. Everyone seemed to stare at the sky, in fact, waiting for the cloud to pass. When the sun returned, the car gave a small jerk, then another jerk, and then it began to roll. It accelerated down the track, and Maya stopped biting her lip and started to cheer.

She finished second out of 18 cars. The winner was an older boy whose car had been built with great care over two years, and Maya, with her instructor beside her, went straight to his table to ask how he had made the wheels so light.

That evening, she told her parents that she felt accomplished, a word she had learned from Mr. Patel. She had not won, but she had accomplished what she set out to do: she had built a car that worked. Had she not failed twice, she said, she would not have known how to succeed.

Questions:
What is the Sunshine Derby?
It is a school race for small cars that run only on power from the sun.
Which trait does Mr. Patel consider most useful in a young engineer?
He considers patience the most useful trait.
Why did Maya make her car lighter?
A tiny panel produces only a little power, so a light car accelerates faster.
What happened when the cloud moved across the sun?
The car did not move, and Maya bit her lip and tried not to stare at the sky.
Why did Maya feel accomplished?
She had built a car that worked, even though she had not won.

lessons.title: The Monks Who Went Solar
lessons.summary: A small community of monks replaces its old diesel generator with solar panels that float on the monastery pond.
lessons.text:
High in the hills, an hour's drive from the nearest town, 9 monks reside in a stone monastery that is almost 200 years old. They grow their own vegetables, keep bees and make candles, which they sell to visitors and online. Brother Thomas, the oldest monk, has resided there for 52 years, and he still walks out every morning to look at the valley below. Visitors often speak of the majesty of the view, and the monks never grow tired of that majesty either.

For most of those years, the monastery had no connection to the power grid. Electricity came from a noisy diesel generator, and in the evenings, the monks often read by the light of candles, partly to save fuel. Candles are their business, after all. Each candle has a cotton wick, and the monks cut each wick by hand. A good wick, Brother Thomas explains, burns slowly and evenly, without smoke.

The monks keep careful records of everything, from the honey they collect to the fuel they buy. Brother Thomas still writes these records in ink, in a heavy book with a green cover. A few years ago, the ink told a clear story: the monastery was spending more on diesel every year, and the generator was getting old.

The younger monks proposed solar panels, but there was a difficulty. The only flat, open ground was the vegetable garden, and nobody wanted to give it up. The solution was the pond. Today, 60 panels float on its surface, held up by plastic frames and tied to the shore. Panels that float on water have an advantage: the water keeps them cool, and cool panels work better than hot ones. They also shade part of the pond, so less water is lost on hot days.

Some visitors worried about storms. The hills get hail several times a year, and in some years the hail is the size of small stones. Panels, however, are tested against hail before they are sold, and when a hard storm came through last summer, not one panel was damaged. The monks, who had watched the hail from the window, rang the bell in thanks.

The generator is silent now except in the longest periods of cloudy weather. Brother Thomas says the new system suits the way the monks try to live, in harmony with the land and with each other. Living in harmony, he adds, also means not having to listen to a diesel engine during evening prayers.

The garden, saved from the panels, is doing well. The monks grow beans, tomatoes and greens full of vitamins, and they give part of the harvest to families in the town. Brother Thomas, who is 81, credits his health to the vegetables, the vitamins and the walk to the pond each morning. He still cuts a wick or two after breakfast, and he still writes in ink.

Questions:
How many monks reside in the monastery?
There are 9 monks who reside there.
Why does a good wick matter?
A good wick burns slowly and evenly, without smoke.
Why did the monks put the panels on the pond?
The only other flat, open ground was the vegetable garden, and nobody wanted to give it up.
What advantage do panels that float on water have?
The water keeps them cool, and cool panels work better than hot ones.
What happened to the panels during the hail storm?
Not one panel was damaged.

lessons.title: The Case of the Missing Cable
lessons.summary: A news report on how thieves stole copper cable from a solar farm, how they were found and what happened in court.
lessons.text:
On a Sunday night in early spring, thieves cut their way through the fence of the Riverside solar farm, about 10 miles north of town. They took no panels. What they wanted was the copper cable that carries electricity from the panels to the grid. By the time the sun rose, around 2 miles of cable were gone, and a large part of the farm had stopped producing power.

The theft was discovered early on Monday morning, when the farm's computers reported that power from the eastern section had fallen to zero. A worker drove out to check and called the police. The dispatcher who took the call sent a car within minutes. Asked later about that morning, she said that a theft from a solar farm was not a typical call. "Usually, people report a stolen bike or a broken window," she said. "Nobody had ever asked me to dispatch an officer to look for missing cable."

The case went to a police investigator, Sarah Kim, who has worked on metal theft for several years. Copper is valuable, she explained, and when its price rises, so does the number of thefts. A thief does not usually keep the metal. He sells it, often to a scrap metal collector, who buys old metal and sells it again. So the investigator began by visiting every collector within 100 miles.

It did not take long. A collector in a nearby town remembered two men who had brought in a large amount of fresh copper cable on Monday afternoon. He had written down their names and the number of their truck, as the law requires. With that information, the investigator found the men within a week.

Both men were arrested and released on bail while they waited for their trial. The judge set the bail high, partly because the theft had cost the farm far more than the price of the copper. Replacing the cable took a month, and during that time, the farm could not sell the power it was producing.

In the end, there was no long trial. Both men decided to plead guilty. A lawyer who attended the hearing as an observer said that people often plead guilty when the evidence is clear, because a judge may give a shorter sentence to someone who admits the crime.

As one observer from the energy industry put it, the case is a reminder that new energy depends on old metal. The Riverside farm has since added cameras and lights along its fence, and the collector who helped the investigator received a letter of thanks from the police.

Questions:
What did the thieves take from the solar farm?
They took about 2 miles of copper cable, but no panels.
Why did the dispatcher find the call unusual?
Nobody had ever asked her to dispatch an officer to look for missing cable.
Why did the investigator visit every scrap metal collector?
A thief usually sells the metal, often to a scrap metal collector.
Why was the bail set high?
The theft had cost the farm far more than the price of the copper.
Why do people often plead guilty when the evidence is clear?
A judge may give a shorter sentence to someone who admits the crime.

lessons.title: The Quiet Bus on Route 9
lessons.summary: A bus driver describes her first year driving one of the town's new electric buses and how her passengers came to like it.
lessons.text:
For 14 years, Linda Moore drove the same diesel bus on Route 9, a loop that connects the hospital, the library, the main shopping street and two neighborhoods on the edge of town. She knew every hill, every stop and most of her passengers by name. Last year, the town replaced her bus with an electric one, and she was not pleased.

"I'll confess I was one of the people who mocked it," she says. "I said it would run out of power halfway up Hospital Hill." Others mocked the new bus too. A local radio host called it "the toy bus", and for a few weeks, some children waved at it as if it were a toy.

The bus did not run out of power. It is charged every night at the depot and has more than enough range for a full day on Route 9. What surprised Linda most was how different it felt to drive. The old bus shook and roared; the new one is almost silent, and it starts and stops smoothly. She no longer goes home with a headache, and she can hear her passengers talk.

Her elderly passengers noticed the change first. Many of them ride to the hospital or the library, and for an elderly rider standing in the aisle, a smooth start matters a great deal. Mrs. Clark, who is 87, told Linda that the new bus was the first one she could ride without holding on with both hands. The floor is also lower, which makes it more convenient for wheelchairs and for parents with small children.

The fare did not change, which was important. The town had promised that the new buses would not mean a higher fare, and elderly riders still pay half fare. A convenient new card system lets passengers pay by touching a reader at the door.

Over the year, Linda found a new rhythm. The day still has the same stops, but its rhythm feels calmer without the noise. She waves to the same people at the same corners, and now they can hear her when she says good morning.

The mayor is careful about how she describes the change. There was no urgent reason to switch, she says. The old buses simply needed replacing, and the electric ones, though more expensive to buy, are cheaper to run and repair. Still, she admits that cleaner air near the hospital and the school was part of the decision, even if it was not urgent.

Not long ago, a diesel bus was the norm everywhere. Electric buses are now quickly becoming the norm in many cities, and the town plans to replace its last two diesel buses sometime next year. Sometime before then, Linda says, she would like to find that radio host and offer him a ride.

Questions:
Why did Linda mock the new bus at first?
She thought it would run out of power halfway up Hospital Hill.
How did the new bus help elderly passengers?
It starts and stops smoothly, so elderly riders can stand without holding on so tightly.
Did the fare change?
No, the fare stayed the same, and elderly riders still pay half fare.
How did the rhythm of Linda's day change?
The day has the same stops, but its rhythm feels calmer without the noise.
When does the town plan to replace its last two diesel buses?
It plans to replace them sometime next year.
